findings.reason: as declared the two nodes are dispatchable concurrently into separate worktrees writing one hook, so whichever lands second finds its guard already present and its negative control mutates code it did not author.
findings.text: §37 has no `plan-section-depends-on` entry and no link, yet its "when its phase is no longer queued" condition is the same pre-launch re-read §35's second deliverable adds to the same function in `reckon/crew/queue_admission.py` (and §35's held arm *is* that condition: `queue_edit._change_hold` sets `current["phase"] = "held"` at `reckon/crew/queue_edit.py:578`)

findings.reason: the one condition §37 adds beyond §35's scope is the only one its own gate cannot show fires, so the gap is untested exactly where the sections overlap.
findings.text: the deliverable requires that a launch is refused when the pointer is gone, when the phase is no longer queued, and when an attempt has exited with a result, while the three cases measure only the first and the second and the third is the unchanged positive path; a node passes all three by implementing the pointer and attempt checks alone and leaving the phase condition out

findings.reason: the mechanism as stated reproduces the failure it repairs on the arm that matters, and the worker needs the destination named (a run-directory record or a pass-level skipped list) before the case can pass.
findings.text: §36's remedy is "when the pointer is gone … it records the run as `landed-elsewhere`", but every landing status in this module is written through `_record_attempt` (`reckon/crew/queue_landing.py:322`), whose `runs._mutate_pointer` call reads the live pointer first (`reckon/crew/runs.py:371`), raising the very `CrewError: no live run` the section exists to remove (`reckon/crew/runs.py:956`); the pointer-gone arm therefore has nowhere to record its verdict as written

response_events.note: §37 drops the phase condition, which §35's held arm owns, leaving the removed-pointer and delivered-attempt arms; §36 records landed-elsewhere on the landing stage's own record, not the vanished pointer

wiring-1.note: §37 drops the phase condition, which §35's held arm owns, leaving the removed-pointer and delivered-attempt arms; §36 records landed-elsewhere on the landing stage's own record, not the vanished pointer

rubric_items.anchors_resolve: pass — `reckon/crew/queue_edit.py` near 594 and 613 are exactly `hold`'s and `release`'s `_admit_lock` acquisitions, `reckon/crew/promotion.py` near 174–231 holds `_promotion_*` lease functions, commit `3d64ca5322` resolves as the cited promote commit, and both `r-20261105T091632392412-…` (cited by its promote commit rather than its now-discarded directory) and `r-20261105T112218135978-…` resolve, the latter holding the `attempt-1-exit.json` and `attempt-1-review-filed.json` it cites.
rubric_items.done_when: a finding — §37's deliverable names three conditions a launch must refuse on, and its done-when measures two; the "phase is no longer queued" condition has no case and no control of its own.
rubric_items.evidence_paths: pass — every gate is a repository test file under `tests/` and every log is stated under the run directory; no case names a scratchpad or a node-local temporary path.
rubric_items.naming: pass — the new test filenames name the mechanism, and `landed-elsewhere` carries no plan label, ticket number or version tag.
rubric_items.reasoning: a finding — §36 records the run as `landed-elsewhere` when the pointer is gone, but the module's only landing-status store writes onto that pointer.
rubric_items.single_goal: pass — §35 (the stage-edit verbs), §36 (the lander) and §37 (the launch) each name one repair on one file pair; the earlier split of §35's launch-staleness arms into §37 is reflected in the section declarations and in §35's pointer to §37.
rubric_items.wiring: a finding — §37 declares `plan-section-depends-on: []` and no `data-links`, yet it adds a pre-launch pointer/phase re-read to the same hook in `reckon/crew/queue_admission.py` that §35's second deliverable adds.
